title: Debugging Techniques
description: Master essential debugging skills for ASP.NET Core applications. Learn to use breakpoints, watch windows, call stacks, and diagnostic tools to find and fix bugs efficiently. Understand how to debug API requests, inspect variables, and trace execution flow.

blocks.text: Debugging is the process of finding and fixing defects in your code. Even experienced developers spend a significant portion of their time debugging. The difference between a slow debugger and a fast one is not talent — it is knowing which tools to use and when to use them.

Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and Rider all include powerful debugging tools. In ASP.NET Core, debugging typically involves tracing the execution of a request through the middleware pipeline, into a controller, through the service layer, and back out again. Each step of that journey is observable with the right techniques.

A breakpoint pauses execution at a specific line of code. When execution reaches the breakpoint, the debugger takes control and lets you inspect the current state of the application. You can examine variable values, step through code line by line, and modify values on the fly. Breakpoints are the most fundamental and most used debugging tool.

In Visual Studio, click the left margin next to a line to set a breakpoint. In VS Code, press F9 on the desired line. Conditional breakpoints pause execution only when a specific condition is true, which is invaluable when a bug only occurs under certain circumstances.

blocks.title: Types of Breakpoints
items: Line Breakpoint: Pauses on a specific line of code — the most common type
Conditional Breakpoint: Pauses only when a condition you define evaluates to true
Tracepoint: Logs a message to the output window without pausing execution — useful for lightweight logging
Hit Count Breakpoint: Pauses only after the line has been hit a specified number of times — useful inside loops
Function Breakpoint: Pauses when a specific method is called, regardless of where in the codebase it is defined

blocks.text: Once paused at a breakpoint, you control execution flow using step commands. Step Into (F11) moves into the method being called, letting you trace into library code. Step Over (F10) executes the current line and moves to the next — useful for skipping over library calls you trust. Step Out (Shift+F11) finishes the current method and returns to its caller.

blocks.title: Use Step Into Selectively
blocks.text: You do not need to step into every method call. Step Into is most valuable for tracing your own application logic. For framework or library methods you trust, use Step Over to save time. If you accidentally step into a large library method, Step Out returns you to your code immediately.

While paused at a breakpoint, hover over any variable to see its current value in a DataTip. For more complex scenarios, add variables to the Watch window so you can monitor them as you step through code. The Locals window shows all variables in the current scope, and the Autos window shows variables used in the current and previous statements.

The Immediate Window lets you execute C# expressions on the fly. You can change variable values, call methods, and evaluate expressions — all while the debugger is paused. This is incredibly powerful for testing hypotheses about what a bug might be without restarting the debugging session.

The Call Stack window shows the chain of method calls that led to the current breakpoint. Each entry represents a method on the stack. You can click any entry to jump to that point in the code and inspect the local variables at that level of the call stack. This is essential for understanding how execution reached a particular point — especially in complex middleware pipelines.
Debugging API Requests in ASP.NET Core

When debugging an API, it helps to understand the full request lifecycle. The request enters through Kestrel, passes through middleware, reaches routing, enters the controller action, calls the service, and returns. Each of these stages is a potential point of failure, and the debugger lets you trace through all of them.

blocks.title: Debugging an API Controller Action
blocks.content: Setting a breakpoint in a controller action and inspecting the incoming request data and model state.

blocks.text: Sometimes the best debugging tool is not a debugger at all — it is structured logging. ASP.NET Core's built-in logging writes messages to the console, debug output, and configured log providers. Using scopes, structured placeholders, and appropriate log levels, you can reconstruct the execution flow of a request without attaching a debugger.

In Visual Studio, the Diagnostic Tools window shows CPU usage, memory allocation, and events while debugging. You can also use the Exception Settings window to configure the debugger to break on specific exceptions the moment they are thrown, rather than waiting for them to bubble up and crash the application.

blocks.title: Break on All Exceptions
blocks.text: In Visual Studio, open Exception Settings (Ctrl+Alt+E) and check 'Common Language Runtime Exceptions'. This makes the debugger break the moment any exception is thrown, even if it is later caught and handled. It is the fastest way to find where an unexpected exception originates.

terms.definition: A marker in code that pauses execution so the developer can inspect program state at that point.
A list of active method calls showing the execution path that led to the current point in the program.
A debugger pane where you can pin specific variables or expressions to monitor their values as you step through code.
A debugger command that moves execution into the next method call, allowing you to trace inside it.
A breakpoint that only triggers when a specified condition is true, reducing noise during debugging.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Debugging Techniques
points: Breakpoints pause execution at a specific line so you can inspect program state
Step Into, Step Over, and Step Out control execution flow while paused at a breakpoint
Watch and Locals windows let you monitor variable values as you step through code
The Call Stack shows the execution path that led to the current breakpoint
Conditional breakpoints and tracepoints reduce noise by targeting specific scenarios
Exception breakpoints stop execution the moment an exception is thrown, before it is caught
blocks.takeaway: Debugging is not guesswork — it is systematic investigation. Breakpoints let you pause and observe, the Call Stack tells you how you got there, and the Watch window shows you what is happening. Combined with structured logging, these tools let you diagnose any issue in an ASP.NET Core application.

blocks.title: Exercise: Debug a Broken API Endpoint
blocks.description: Practice debugging techniques by finding and fixing bugs in a deliberately flawed API controller.
steps: Create a ProductsController with three intentional bugs: an off-by-one ID error, a null reference when the product is missing, and a wrong status code on delete
Set a conditional breakpoint on the GetById action that triggers only when id > 100
Use the Call Stack window to trace how the request reached the controller
Use the Watch window to inspect the product variable returned from the service
Use the Immediate Window to call the service directly and compare results
Enable breaking on all exceptions and identify which exception is thrown and where
blocks.expectedOutcome: All three bugs identified using debugger tools: the conditional breakpoint catches the off-by-one case, the Watch window reveals the null reference, and the Exception Settings window catches the unhandled exception on delete.

items.text: I can set and use breakpoints in Visual Studio or VS Code
items.hint: Click the margin or press F9. Execution pauses so you can inspect state.

items.text: I know the difference between Step Into, Step Over, and Step Out
items.hint: Step Into (F11) enters methods. Step Over (F10) runs the current line. Step Out (Shift+F11) finishes the current method.

items.text: I can use the Watch window to monitor variable values
items.hint: Right-click a variable and select 'Add Watch', or type the expression directly in the Watch pane.

items.text: I understand how to use the Call Stack to trace execution flow
items.hint: The Call Stack shows each method call in the current execution path — click any entry to jump to that code.

items.text: I know how to make the debugger break on exceptions automatically
items.hint: Open Exception Settings (Ctrl+Alt+E) and check Common Language Runtime Exceptions.
